newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: ASIAN EXOTICS - Regionals little moved by Fed.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN EXOTICS - Regionals little moved by Fed.

text.p: Southeast Asian currencies showed little immediate reaction on Wednesday to the U.S. Federal Reserve's overnight move to hike short-term interest rates by 25 basis points.
Dealers said the rate hike had been discounted by the market and activity in regional currencies was being driven by domestic liquidity conditions and speculative fund flows.

"What happens to U.S. rates will not have a direct effect on regional currencies. But given time, these countries will have to hike rates as well because inflation will start creeping up," said a senior bank dealer in Singapore.
Only the Thai baht slid sharply as local banks moved to buy dollars on the back of the U.S. rate hike, Bangkok dealers said.

"Dollar carrying costs are very low right now so the banks prefer dollars to baht ... The market was active early as people took positions after the Fed rise but I think most of the action is over now," said a dealer at Thai Danu Bank.
The baht was quoted at 26.006/26.010 to the dollar at 0430 GMT compared with 25.985/25.990 late on Tuesday. The central bank set the mid-rate at 25.99 against 25.96 on Tuesday.
Market reaction to the rate rise, which puts upward pressure on domestic rates, was beginning to subside and the baht was expected to track majors for the rest of the day, dealers said.
They said liquidity was still high as cash from new provident and pension funds remained in the market.

Research firm I.D.E.A. said in a daily market commentary that interbank rates were threatening to slip as low as three percent when 80 billion baht worth of government pension funds were fully released into the market.
In Malaysia, the ringgit recovered from its morning lows on fresh U.S. fund buying of the ringgit/Singapore dollar cross.

Dealers said the market was scarcely affected by the U.S. rate hike and focused instead on the upcoming release of Bank Negara's annual report, with rumours of a further tightening of monetary policy keeping the ringgit underpinned.
"Malaysian interest rates are still 150-200 basis points higher than in the U.S. So funds are still interested in Malaysia," said a dealer with a Malaysian bank in Kuala Lumpur.
"This is making the Singapore dollar more unattractive and encouraging funds to move into ringgit. Moreover, the recent inflow has mostly been from the Singapore dollar," he said.
The Singapore dollar fell below the 1.4400 level to the U.S. dollar again as buying of the ringgit/Sing cross from an opening around 0.5810 took the wind out of the Singapore dollar.
"Dollar/Sing should move between 1.4430 and 1.4480 today but I believe it still needs to reach 1.4500. Some people are even calling for 1.4600," said the Singapore-based dealer.
The Singapore dollar was at 1.4437/47 to the U.S. unit at 0430 GMT. The ringgit/Sing cross was at 0.5829/34.
In Indonesia, the rupiah remained firmly underpinned amid tight liquidity with the 1996/97 financial year end looming on March 31.
Banks have only one more day to settle outstanding taxes as the market will be closed on Friday for a public holiday and on Monday for the fiscal year-end, reopening on April 1.

"I can't detect any changes in market sentiment. People are still bullish on the rupiah," a local bank dealer in Jakarta said. "But the dollar is well supported at the 2,397.0 level. Attempts to break this support level have failed," he added.
Spot rupiah was at 2,398.70/99.50 at 0430 GMT, compared with an opening of 2,398.00/98.25.
A Japanese bank dealer said the dollar could be poised to rebound gradually when liquidity turned around.
-- Reme Ahmad in Kuala Lumpur (603-230 8911), Mantik Kusjanto in Jakarta (6221-384-6364), Anuchit Nguyen in Bangkok (662) 652-0642 and Sonali Desai in Singapore (65-8703090)
